items.prompt: A message asks three teams to fix their retry logic. What is it missing?
choices: An owner, a deadline and an artifact
A longer technical explanation
A louder or more urgent tone
items.explanation: Without an owner or deadline, nothing turns the request into scheduled work.

items.prompt: Does an accurate message guarantee change?
choices: Yes, true statements get acted on
No, accuracy alone schedules nothing
Yes, if it is posted in a public channel
items.explanation: Being right is not the bottleneck; getting it onto someone's plan is.

items.prompt: Why would a team ignore a correct warning about a bug they have not hit?
choices: Teams never trust other teams
The warning is probably false
It competes with work they are already committed to
items.explanation: Unscheduled work loses to the backlog the team is already accountable for.

items.prompt: Which is most likely to get a team to change its code?
choices: A merged, working example they can copy
A reminder in the weekly announcements
A request to be more careful
items.explanation: A concrete artifact lowers the cost of acting; a reminder does not.

items.prompt: Dana has no authority over the other teams. What does that rule out?
choices: Writing code
Assigning them the work
Reviewing pull requests
items.explanation: She can still contribute and review; she just cannot assign.

items.prompt: In the scenario, what made the retry bug costly during incidents?
choices: The library was too slow
The tests were failing
Doomed requests kept adding load
items.explanation: Retrying a request that cannot succeed only loads a struggling service.

items.prompt: What does 'someone's Tuesday' stand for in this unit?
choices: A task actually scheduled for a person
A weekly meeting slot
A deadline set by a manager
items.explanation: It marks the gap between a real problem and work someone owns.

items.prompt: Which situation is closest to a Slack message asking everyone to be more careful?
choices: A ticket assigned to one named person
A poster asking everyone to remember a rule
A failing test in CI
items.explanation: Both are general, ownerless requests that rely on memory and goodwill.

items.prompt: A staff-wide post says 'please audit your services for unsafe retries.' Two weeks later nothing has changed. What best explains it?
choices: The post named a problem but gave nobody a scheduled task to complete
Engineers generally dislike being asked to audit their own services
The post should have been emailed to each team lead one by one
The audit was too small a task to be worth anyone's attention, given how much else the teams had going on
items.explanation: The request had no owner, deadline or artifact, so it never became anyone's planned work.
items.reference:
Why announcements stall
📣 announcement: correct, but no owner or deadline
📄 PR + RFC: an artifact people can act on
🗓️ unscheduled work competes with every backlog
Why: being right does not get work scheduled; something has to turn a true statement into a task someone owns.
items.learnMore:
Correct is not the same as actionable

A message can be accurate and still change nothing. Each team has its own priorities and already-working code, so a request with no owner, no deadline and nothing to point at becomes optional work that never gets scheduled.

Common mistake

Assuming people will act on a problem just because it was explained clearly once.
items.reflection: Think of a group chat message that everyone agreed with and nobody acted on. What would have had to exist for someone to actually do it?

items.prompt: Dana's warning is accurate, and a team lead agrees with it in a thread. Why is that still not progress?

Threads are rarely read by teams other than the author's
Agreement only counts when it comes from a manager
Agreement puts no change on the team's plan
items.explanation: Nothing yet has been scheduled, assigned or merged, so behavior is unchanged.

items.prompt: A teammate sends a clear RFC but has never worked with the other teams and has no working fix. Which channels are missing?
choices: Writing and review
Code and relationships
Review alone, since the rest are covered
None, because an RFC covers all four jobs
items.explanation: There is no proof the idea works and no trust to get it read.
items.reference:
Four channels of influence
💻 code: proof it works
📝 writing: a citable plan
🔍 review: nudges at the right moment
🤝 relationships: why it gets read
Why: each channel does a job the others cannot, so using only one leaves a gap.
items.learnMore:
Four jobs, four channels

Code shows the idea works, writing makes it durable and shareable, review delivers it at the moment of use, and relationships decide whether the first three get attention. Dana used all four in sequence.

Common mistake

Treating one channel, usually the written proposal, as the whole job.

Relationships: proving the fix survives real traffic

items.prompt: Which is the best evidence Dana's influence worked?
choices: Several people praised the RFC
A lead said it sounded good
Another team merged a change using the library
items.explanation: Merged behavior change is the outcome.

items.prompt: Is 'Great RFC!' a sign of influence?
choices: No, agreement costs nothing
Yes, it proves people read it
Yes, it proves adoption
items.explanation: Praise is compatible with no change.

items.prompt: What is a stronger signal than a merged PR Dana asked for?
choices: A longer RFC thread
A new PR using the library without being asked
A calendar invite for a meeting
items.explanation: Unprompted use shows the pattern spread.

items.prompt: A lead says 'I'll look into it.' What does that show?
choices: Adoption
A decision to reject
Intent, not a change
items.explanation: Nothing in the code has changed yet.

items.prompt: After six weeks, what existed in the scenario?
choices: Three teams using one shared library
Three approved tickets
Three signed agreements
items.explanation: The proof was in the codebases.

items.prompt: Why is thumbs-up a weak measure?
choices: It is hard to give
It requires no change in behavior
It cannot be seen by others
items.explanation: Cheap signals can be given without doing anything.

items.prompt: Which question tests whether influence worked?
choices: Did people say they liked it?
Was the thread long?
Is the code different now?
items.explanation: The test is behavior in the code.

items.prompt: What would a revert of the adoption PR indicate?
choices: The influence did not hold
The influence was strongest
Nothing at all
items.explanation: Adoption must persist to count.

items.prompt: An RFC gets forty approving reactions and no code changes. How should Dana read this?
choices: As strong adoption, since people took time to react
As proof that the RFC is technically perfect
As agreement without any evidence of influence
As a sign that the teams will adopt next month
items.explanation: Reactions cost nothing; the codebases are unchanged.
items.reference:
Adoption as proof
👍 praise and agreement: cheap
🗣️ 'will look into it': intent only
✅ merged PR using the library: behavior changed
🌱 new PR using it unprompted: it spread
Why: only changed behavior shows influence worked; agreement and praise are compatible with nothing changing.
items.learnMore:
Measure what changed, not what was said

Positive comments cost nothing to give. A merged change in another team's code, and especially a new change that uses the pattern without being asked, is evidence the idea moved from your head into their practice.

Common mistake

Counting enthusiasm in a thread as success.
items.reflection: Think of a habit you tried to get others to adopt. What would you have looked for to know it actually stuck?

Dana's own PR is merged in her home team's code

items.prompt: What does a working fix prove that an argument cannot?
choices: That it holds up under real conditions
That the author is confident
That the topic is important
items.explanation: It has met real edge cases and traffic.

items.prompt: A proposal with no working code reads as...
choices: A finished design
Untested opinion
A formal decision
items.explanation: Readers cannot tell if it survives reality.

items.prompt: Why did Dana fix it in payments first?
choices: To avoid writing an RFC
Because payments owned the library
To have running proof before asking others
items.explanation: The working fix backed the later proposal.

items.prompt: What did the tests in the fix provide?
choices: Falsifiable claims about behavior
Style guidance
A deadline for adoption
items.explanation: Tests are runnable assertions, harder to dismiss than prose.

items.prompt: Which is cheaper for a busy reader to judge?
choices: A hypothetical design
A concrete merged change
A verbal pitch
items.explanation: Concrete things are easier to evaluate than imagined ones.

items.prompt: Design debates about edge cases are often...
choices: Impossible to settle
Only settled by managers
Settled by what the code had to handle
items.explanation: Implementation exposes the real cases.

items.prompt: When is code-first the better default?
choices: When you are already confident in the fix
When nobody knows the problem
When the design is wide open
items.explanation: Confidence and a known direction justify building first.

items.prompt: Which opening is stronger for an RFC?
choices: Here is an idea; thoughts?
Here is a working fix; consider adopting it
Please approve this plan
items.explanation: It lets readers judge something real.

items.prompt: Dana is sure her retry fix is right, but a colleague wants RFC-first to gather opinions. What does code-first give her?
choices: A way to sidestep feedback from the other teams
Authority over how the other teams spend their time and so make the objection window in the RFC redundant
A shorter RFC that no longer needs an objection window
A concrete fix to react to, with design questions tested on real cases
items.explanation: It converts an open debate into a review of something working.
items.reference:
Code before proposal
💻 working fix: proof under real conditions
📝 proposal alone: untested opinion
⚖️ exception: genuinely open decisions
Why: a working fix is cheaper to evaluate than an argument for one, and settles design questions through real constraints.
items.learnMore:
Proof beats persuasion

A merged, tested fix answers many hypothetical questions by existing. It moves the conversation from whether the idea could work to whether to adopt something that already works.

Common mistake

Opening with a proposal when you already have enough confidence to build a small proof.
items.reflection: Think of a time you showed a rough prototype instead of describing an idea. How did the response differ?

The pattern will be adopted far faster than it should
Readers treat it as untested opinion and deprioritize it
Nobody will manage to find the document at all
items.explanation: Without proof, readers have no reason to trust the claim.

The RFC as a durable artifact

items.prompt: A teammate with strong credibility wants to build a new shared cache layer, but three teams have different caching needs. Which order is better?
choices: Build first, so that credibility carries the result
Skip discussion entirely in order to move faster
Gather input on needs first, then build
Ship to everyone and write the RFC afterward
items.explanation: Open design space and differing needs favor input first.
items.reference:
When to gather input first
🧪 strong evidence + trusted fix → code first
🧭 several open directions → input first
👥 affected people hold context → input first
Why: code-first assumes enough conviction to build something worth reacting to; when it is missing, input first avoids sunk effort.
items.learnMore:
Match the order to the decision

Code-first suits a well-understood fix. If the design space is open, or others hold the key context, a short options memo and conversation first can redirect work before it is built.

Common mistake

Treating code-first as a rule instead of a default that depends on how settled the decision is.
items.reflection: Think of a project where you built first and learned too late what mattered to others. What question could you have asked up front?
